unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Ashvale Ceramics Ltd is a private limited company that imports and wholesales glazed wall tiles across Country X. The business has traded for 9 years, employs 26 staff and generates $3,400,000 in annual revenue. Around 60% of its stock, worth $400,000 each year, is bought from Country Z, which lies outside the Celestra Trade Bloc of which Country X is a member.

From next quarter, the Country X government will raise the import tariff on wall tiles from Country Z from 10% to 25%. Domestic tile makers, who already supply 40% of Ashvale's stock, welcome the protection. Management must now decide whether to switch entirely to domestic suppliers or keep importing from Country Z and pass the extra $60,000 annual cost on to retail customers, who currently pay $45 per box.

questions.question_text: Define 'import tariff'.
questions.model_answer: A tax placed on goods or services brought into a country, increasing their price to buyers [2].

knowledge_max_2: A tax on imports / goods brought into a country
Raises the price of the imported good / protects domestic industry

questions.question_text: Explain two impacts on Ashvale Ceramics Ltd of the tariff rising from 10% to 25%.
questions.model_answer: Impact 1: Raised import costs [k], adding about $60,000 a year to the $400,000 of Country Z stock Ashvale buys annually [app]. Impact 2: Improved price competitiveness of domestic tiles [k], allowing Ashvale to sell more of the 40% domestic stock it already handles [app].

knowledge_max_2: Tariff raises the cost/price of imports
Tariff makes domestic goods relatively more competitive
application_max_2: $400,000 of Country Z stock; the 15 percentage point rise adds about $60,000 a year
Domestic tiles already supply 40% of stock so this share can grow

questions.question_text: Explain two ways the higher tariff could affect Ashvale Ceramics' retail customers.
questions.model_answer: Way 1: Higher retail prices for imported tiles [k], as Ashvale passes on the extra $60,000 a year to shoppers paying $45 per box [app], leaving customers with less disposable income for other purchases [an]. Way 2: Reduced choice on the shelves [k], because fewer Country Z tile lines will be stocked from next quarter [app], so customers may not find the exact style or size they want [an].

knowledge_max_2: Prices of imported goods rise when a tariff is charged
Range/stock of imported goods falls
application_max_2: Extra $60,000 a year passed on; customers pay $45 per box
Country Z lines will be restocked less often from next quarter
analysis_max_2: Households have less disposable income / switch spending elsewhere
Customers cannot find desired styles and may shop elsewhere

questions.question_text: Do you think Ashvale Ceramics Ltd should switch entirely to domestic suppliers or continue importing tiles from Country Z? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: One option is to switch entirely to domestic suppliers, which would remove the $60,000 yearly tariff cost [k]; with domestic tiles already supplying 40% of stock, Ashvale could expand buying from proven local makers and protect its $3,400,000 revenue [app]. This would cut delivery lead times and reduce exposure to further tariff changes [an]. The alternative is to keep importing from Country Z, preserving the wide glazed wall tile range that customers pay $45 per box for [app]; margins would shrink as the duty rises to 25%, so prices may need to rise [an]. Imported goods face higher costs when governments use tariffs to protect local industry [k]. Overall, switching entirely to domestic suppliers is better because the 25% tariff is confirmed for next quarter and saving $60,000 a year directly improves profit [eval], although keeping a small premium import line could retain choice-conscious customers [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Domestic suppliers avoid the import tariff cost
Tariffs raise the cost of imported goods above domestic alternatives
application_max_2: $60,000 yearly cost removed; domestic tiles already 40% of stock
Country Z range preserved; $45 per box; 25% duty from next quarter
analysis_max_2: Shorter lead times and lower risk of further tariff rises
Margins shrink and shop prices may have to rise for imported styles
evaluation_max_2: Reaches a justified overall judgement using stem figures
Weighs the trade-off and qualifies the recommendation

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Hollinbrook Poultry Ltd is a family-owned chicken farm and processing business in rural Country X. It has operated for 11 years, employs 45 workers and sells 9,000 chickens every week at an average of $4.50 per kilogram, generating $6,000,000 in annual revenue. The farm is running at 85% of its housing capacity and already supplies several national supermarket chains with fresh chicken each week.

The Country X government has announced that the import quota for chicken meat will fall from 8,000 tonnes to 3,000 tonnes a year, to protect domestic producers. Imported frozen chicken, previously cheaper at $3.20 per kilogram, will become scarcer in supermarkets. Hollinbrook could invest $1,200,000 in two new sheds to house 2,500 more birds a week, or continue at its current output.

questions.question_text: Define 'import quota'.
questions.model_answer: A physical limit on the quantity of a good that a country allows to be imported [2].

knowledge_max_2: A limit on the quantity/amount of an import
Restricts how much of the good may enter the country

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits for Hollinbrook Poultry Ltd of the government cutting the chicken import quota from 8,000 to 3,000 tonnes.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Reduced competition from imports [k], so supermarkets seeking chicken at around $4.50 per kilogram are more likely to contract Hollinbrook's 9,000 weekly birds [app]. Benefit 2: Opportunity to raise price or output [k], as scarce supply lets the farm push up margins or fill its 85% capacity with extra orders [app].

knowledge_max_2: Limiting import supply reduces foreign competition for domestic firms
Domestic firms can sell more and/or charge higher prices when imports are capped
application_max_2: 9,000 chickens a week at $4.50 offered to supermarkets
Farm only at 85% capacity so room to raise sales

questions.question_text: Explain two limitations of relying on the import quota for Hollinbrook Poultry Ltd's success.
questions.model_answer: Limitation 1: The quota could be relaxed later [k], so demand for Hollinbrook's chicken could fall back to supermarkets' previous import mix [app], leaving the farm with half-empty sheds and falling capacity utilisation [an]. Limitation 2: Protection reduces pressure to improve efficiency [k], so the farm may not tackle its $6,000,000 cost base as it would under import competition [app], meaning it struggles on price if the 3,000-tonne protection ends [an].

knowledge_max_2: Quotas can be temporary and removed later
Protection removes the incentive to improve efficiency / cut costs
application_max_2: If imports return to 8,000 tonnes, supermarket demand for domestic chicken falls
Revenue of $6,000,000 without cost pressure from cheaper $3.20 imports
analysis_max_2: Idle sheds / falling capacity utilisation if demand slips
Uncompetitive prices once protection ends / lower long-term profit

questions.question_text: Do you think Hollinbrook Poultry Ltd should invest $1,200,000 in two new sheds to increase output or maintain its current output? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Investing $1,200,000 in two new sheds would raise capacity by 2,500 birds a week [k]; with imported chicken capped at 3,000 tonnes a year, supermarket demand is likely to shift to domestic suppliers such as Hollinbrook's 9,000-bird weekly output [app], lifting revenue above $6,000,000 and pushing capacity past 85% [an]. However, maintaining current output avoids the $1,200,000 cost and any debt risk [k]; if the quota is relaxed or demand softens, the extra sheds would sit empty and cut profit [app], leaving the farm with weak cash flow [an]. Overall, investing in the sheds is the better option because the quota cut from 8,000 to 3,000 tonnes is a confirmed government policy and the gain comes through sales of 2,500 extra birds a week [eval], although the board should secure supermarket contracts before building begins [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Expansion increases capacity/output
Maintaining output avoids large capital spending / debt
application_max_2: 2,500 extra birds a week; quota capped at 3,000 tonnes
$1,200,000 cost; quota could be relaxed
analysis_max_2: Revenue rises above $6,000,000; capacity utilisation improves beyond 85%
Idle sheds and weak cash flow if demand falls back
evaluation_max_2: Overall justified judgement tied to the confirmed quota cut
Acknowledges condition/uncertainty before recommending

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Willow & Whistle Toys is an independent toy shop in the town of Millbrook, Country X, a founding member of the Orin Trade Bloc. The two-storey shop has traded for 13 years, employs 11 staff and generates $2,100,000 in annual revenue across 4,000 square metres of retail space.

About 70% of stock comes from outside the Orin Trade Bloc. The government has confirmed an 18% import tariff plus an annual quota of 200,000 toy units on non-bloc imports, down from unlimited entry. Bloc-made toys enter tariff-free but cost about 12% more at wholesale and come in a narrower range. Management expects the average shelf price of an imported toy to rise from $50 to $59, while overall choice on the shelves will shrink.

questions.question_text: Define 'trade bloc'.
questions.model_answer: A group of countries that agree to reduce or remove trade barriers between members to encourage trade [2].

knowledge_max_2: A group of countries trading together
Trade barriers between members are reduced or removed

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the 18% import tariff on Willow & Whistle Toys.
questions.model_answer: Effect 1: Higher cost of imported stock [k], since the average shelf price of an imported toy rises from $50 to $59 under the 18% tariff [app]. Effect 2: Greater appeal of bloc-made toys [k], which enter the Orin Trade Bloc tariff-free and so become more price-competitive in the shop's range [app].

knowledge_max_2: A tariff raises the price of imported goods
Tariffs improve the competitiveness of goods from inside the bloc
application_max_2: Average imported toy price rises from $50 to $59
Bloc-made toys enter tariff-free and become comparatively cheaper

questions.question_text: Explain two ways the import quota of 200,000 toy units could affect the shop's customers.
questions.model_answer: Way 1: Fewer toys available on the shelves [k], as only 200,000 non-bloc units may enter Country X each year [app], so popular imported lines may sell out as families shop for birthdays [an]. Way 2: Less product choice for shoppers [k], because the shop cannot restock its usual import-heavy range and must narrow the 70% of stock sourced from outside the Orin Trade Bloc [app], leaving customers with fewer styles and brands [an].

knowledge_max_2: A quota caps the volume of imports available
Reduced import supply reduces customer choice / availability
application_max_2: Only 200,000 non-bloc toy units may enter each year
70% of stock comes from outside the Orin Trade Bloc
analysis_max_2: Popular lines sell out / customers cannot buy wanted toys
Narrower range means shoppers switch to other shops

questions.question_text: Do you think Willow & Whistle Toys should switch to mainly bloc-made toys or keep its current import-heavy range? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Switching to mainly bloc-made toys removes the 18% tariff cost [k]; since tariff-free bloc toys are only about 12% more expensive at wholesale, the shop's shelf prices would stay closer to $50 levels while protecting margins [app]. This also strengthens ties with bloc suppliers and guarantees supply under the quota [an]. However, keeping the import-heavy range preserves the variety customers value, with 70% of stock from outside the Orin Trade Bloc [app]; the 200,000-unit quota and the $59 price point will squeeze sales and margins [an]. Import duties raise consumer prices and reduce choice when stocked goods come from outside a trade bloc [k]. Overall, switching to mainly bloc-made toys is better because the quota and 18% tariff are confirmed, whereas the 12% wholesale premium is modest against avoiding a $9 price rise per toy [eval], although the shop should keep a small import range for loyal customers [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Bloc-made goods enter tariff-free inside the bloc
Tariffs raise consumer prices and reduce choice
application_max_2: Tariff-free toys only 12% dearer at wholesale vs $59 price point
70% of stock from outside bloc; 200,000-unit quota confirmed
analysis_max_2: Secures supply and protects margins within the quota
Import range squeezes sales and margins as prices rise to $59
evaluation_max_2: Clear, justified overall recommendation with figures
Recognises conditions under which keeping some imports still works

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Vesper Electronics Assembly Ltd is a private limited company that assembles consumer audio equipment in Country X. The factory has operated for 8 years, employs 210 workers and generates $14,000,000 in annual revenue. Around 55% of output, worth $7,700,000 a year, is exported to members of the Meridia Free Trade Area, a bloc of 8 countries with 190 million consumers.

Country X is not a member of the Meridia Free Trade Area, so Vesper's exports face a 16% tariff, costing roughly $1,232,000 a year. Management is weighing whether to build a new assembly plant in Country W, a Meridia member, at a cost of $6,500,000, or to keep producing in Country X and absorb the tariff. Either way, the board wants to protect its position in the bloc's growing electronics market.

questions.question_text: Define 'globalisation'.
questions.model_answer: The process by which businesses and economies become increasingly connected and interdependent across national borders [2].

knowledge_max_2: Businesses operating across national borders
Growing interconnection of world economies

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits for Vesper Electronics Assembly Ltd of building the plant in Country W.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Tariff-free access to Meridia members [k], removing the 16% tariff on $7,700,000 of exports and saving about $1,232,000 a year [app]. Benefit 2: Closer access to 190 million consumers [k], cutting delivery times and transport costs for the audio equipment sold across the 8 Meridia countries [app].

knowledge_max_2: Bloc membership means tariff-free trade between members
Locating in a market reduces delivery times and transport costs
application_max_2: Removes 16% duty on $7,700,000 of exports; saves about $1,232,000 a year
8 member countries; 190 million consumers close to the new plant

questions.question_text: Explain two problems for Vesper Electronics Assembly Ltd of relocating to Country W.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: High set-up costs [k], as the new Country W plant requires $6,500,000 of capital investment before any revenue is earned [app], stretching cash flow and raising financial risk for the company [an]. Problem 2: Redundancy and disruption at the Country X factory [k], where 210 workers face job losses or transfer to Country W [app], lowering morale and disrupting output during the transition [an].

knowledge_max_2: Relocating requires major capital investment / set-up costs
Relocation can cause redundancies and disruption for the workforce
application_max_2: $6,500,000 to build the Country W plant
210 Country X workers face redundancy or relocation
analysis_max_2: Stretched cash flow / higher financial risk
Low morale and disrupted output during transition

questions.question_text: Do you think Vesper Electronics Assembly Ltd should build the new assembly plant in Country W or keep producing in Country X? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Building the Country W plant eliminates the 16% tariff [k], saving roughly $1,232,000 a year on $7,700,000 of exports and giving tariff-free sales across the 8 Meridia countries with 190 million consumers [app]; output closer to customers would also cut freight costs and delivery times [an]. However, remaining in Country X avoids the $6,500,000 set-up cost [k], keeps the 210 existing workers in place and preserves relations with national government [app], but the tariff would keep eroding margins every year [an]. Overall, Vesper should build the Country W plant because the annual tariff saving and bloc market access justify the investment over time [eval], although a phased relocation that keeps a small Country X line would reduce disruption [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Locating inside the bloc removes the import tariff
Staying avoids relocation/set-up costs and redundancies
application_max_2: $1,232,000 yearly saving; $7,700,000 exports; 190 million consumers
$6,500,000 build cost; 210 Country X workers kept in place
analysis_max_2: Lower freight costs and faster delivery to bloc customers
Continued tariff erodes margins if production stays in Country X
evaluation_max_2: Overall justified judgement with stem figures
Weighs both options and suggests a managed approach

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Orchard & Oak Preserves Co is a jam and chutney producer based in Country X. The firm has operated for 10 years, employs 38 staff and generates $1,800,000 in annual revenue, with 70% of sales in the home market. It currently exports roughly 30% of output to Country Y, a partner in the Trident Trade Bloc, where tariff-free free trade applies.

A new inquiry has revealed that Country Z, a market of 60 million consumers, would consider stocking its products, but Country Z sits outside the Trident Trade Bloc and would charge a 12% import tariff, adding about $1.80 to each $15 case. Country Y offers only 25 million consumers but tariff-free access and a distributor keen to double orders to 48,000 cases a year. Management must decide where to concentrate export growth next year.

questions.question_text: Define 'free trade'.
questions.model_answer: Trade between countries without restrictions such as tariffs or quotas [2].

knowledge_max_2: Trade without barriers between countries
No tariffs or quotas are charged on imports/exports

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits for Orchard & Oak Preserves Co of free trade within the Trident Trade Bloc.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: No tariff on exports to members [k], so the 30% of output sent to Country Y enters without duty on each case [app]. Benefit 2: Easier access to bloc markets [k], helping Orchard & Oak negotiate larger orders, such as Country Y's distributor doubling purchases to 48,000 cases a year, lifting sales beyond the $1,800,000 revenue [app].

knowledge_max_2: No tariffs within the bloc lowers export costs
Bloc membership improves market access / negotiation power
application_max_2: 30% of output exported to Country Y tariff-free
Distributor doubling orders to 48,000 cases a year; revenue $1,800,000

questions.question_text: Explain two problems for Orchard & Oak Preserves Co of exporting to Country Z instead.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: The 12% tariff adds $1.80 to each $15 case [k], raising the delivered price for Country Z retailers and squeezing Orchard & Oak Preserves Co's export margin [app], which may force the firm to raise prices and lose competitiveness against local makers [an]. Problem 2: No established distributor in Country Z [k], meaning distribution, promotion and transport must be built from scratch in a market of 60 million consumers [app], increasing start-up costs and delaying break-even on export sales [an].

knowledge_max_2: An import tariff raises the price of foreign goods
Entering a new foreign market has set-up costs / needs distribution
application_max_2: $1.80 added to each $15 case at 12% tariff
60 million consumers; no named distributor unlike Country Y
analysis_max_2: Higher shelf prices lose sales to local competitors
Slower break-even / higher start-up cost burden

questions.question_text: Do you think Orchard & Oak Preserves Co should focus export growth on Country Z despite the 12% tariff, or increase sales in Country Y? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Country Z offers 60 million consumers [k], potentially dwarfing Country Y's 25 million, and even after the 12% tariff adds $1.80 to each $15 case, the larger market could absorb big orders and lift export revenue above the current $1,800,000 turnover [app]; however, entering from scratch means distribution costs and no guarantee of listings [an]. Increasing sales in Country Y keeps tariff-free free trade access and a distributor ready to double orders to 48,000 cases a year [app], raising reliable export volume with no duty risk [an]. Tariffs raise export costs and can make promising foreign markets unprofitable [k]. Overall, Orchard & Oak should prioritise Country Y because tariff-free access and the named distributor give the safest growth [eval], although it can test Country Z with a small pilot order before committing [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Large markets with tariffs still carry price/margin penalties
Tariffs raise export costs and reduce profitability
application_max_2: Country Z: 60 million consumers; $1.80 added to each $15 case
Country Y: tariff-free; distributor ready to double to 48,000 cases
analysis_max_2: Country Z entry costs and no listing guarantee
Country Y offers reliable, risk-free volume growth
evaluation_max_2: Clear overall recommendation supported by figures
Qualifies the recommendation with a measured alternative

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Dunfell Steel Rolling Co is a public limited company operating a rolling mill in northern Country X. The mill has run for 17 years, employs 340 workers and produces reinforcing bar for construction firms, with annual revenue of $12,000,000. Capacity utilisation stands at 60%, leaving room to expand output. Around 20% of sales, worth $2,400,000, go to Country Y.

The Country X government is considering a 30% tariff on imported steel to protect domestic producers. Supporters claim the tariff would shield the industry and its jobs, but critics note it may raise prices for construction firms and prompt Country Y to retaliate against Country X exports. Dunfell's directors must decide whether to back the proposal, covering a steel import market worth $90,000,000 a year, or oppose it openly.

questions.question_text: Define 'protectionism'.
questions.model_answer: Government action, such as tariffs or quotas, to restrict imports and shelter domestic producers from foreign competition [2].

knowledge_max_2: Government action to restrict imports (tariffs, quotas)
Aims to shelter domestic producers from foreign competition

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits for Dunfell Steel Rolling Co of the proposed 30% tariff on imported steel.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Reduced foreign competition [k], making Dunfell's reinforcing bar more competitive than imported steel, which would cost 30% more [app]. Benefit 2: Higher sales volumes [k], with the mill at 60% capacity, construction firms could shift rebar orders to Dunfell, raising output and its $12,000,000 revenue [app].

knowledge_max_2: Tariff raises import prices so domestic goods undercut them
Domestic producers can increase sales volumes
application_max_2: Imported steel costs 30% more than Dunfell's reinforcing bar
Mill only at 60% capacity so room to lift output and $12,000,000 revenue

questions.question_text: Explain two limitations of the proposed 30% tariff for Dunfell Steel Rolling Co.
questions.model_answer: Limitation 1: Risk of retaliation by Country Y [k], which buys $2,400,000 of Dunfell's steel each year and could impose its own tariff in response [app], costing Dunfell part of its export business and forcing the mill to find new buyers [an]. Limitation 2: Higher steel prices for construction firms [k], which could dampen building activity in Country X [app], cutting demand for Dunfell's reinforcing bar and leaving the mill short of orders [an].

knowledge_max_2: Tariffs can provoke retaliation from trading partners
Tariffs raise input/output prices and can reduce demand
application_max_2: Country Y buys $2,400,000 of exports; could retaliate
Construction firms pay more for reinforcing bar
analysis_max_2: Export sales lost / need new markets
Demand for the mill's output falls / under-utilised capacity

questions.question_text: Do you think the government should introduce the 30% tariff on imported steel, considering Dunfell Steel Rolling Co? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: The 30% tariff would shelter Dunfell Steel Rolling Co from cheaper foreign steel [k], allowing its reinforcing bar to win orders at a mill running at only 60% capacity, supporting 340 workers and part of its $12,000,000 revenue [app]; protecting home industry should lift domestic output and employment [an]. However, protecting an industry can breed complacency, letting inefficient firms survive without cutting costs [k]. Country Y, which buys $2,400,000 of Dunfell's output, could retaliate with its own tariff [app], costing Dunfell export sales and profits [an]. Overall, on balance the tariff is more likely to harm Dunfell in the long run because retaliation would wipe out the $2,400,000 export stream and customer prices would rise across a $90,000,000 market [eval], although in the short term the mill would gain orders and capacity use [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Tariffs protect domestic producers from foreign competition
Protection can reduce the incentive to improve efficiency
application_max_2: 60% capacity; 340 workers; $12,000,000 revenue
Country Y buys $2,400,000 of exports; $90,000,000 steel market
analysis_max_2: Short-run boost to output, jobs and domestic capacity use
Retaliation and higher prices cut demand and export profit
evaluation_max_2: Balanced judgement reaching a clear conclusion
Weighs short-term gain against long-term harm using figures

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Kingsley Motor Group Plc is a multinational company with assembly plants in 5 countries. Its Country X plant has operated for 14 years, employs 1,800 workers and builds 24,000 vehicles a year, generating $480,000,000 in revenue. Country X sits inside the Valdonia Customs Union, whose members charge a 12% tariff on vehicle parts imported from outside the union.

Kingsley imports engines and gearboxes from Country F, outside the union, at a cost of $60,000,000 a year, paying $7,200,000 in tariffs. A union-based supplier has quoted a price 15% higher, about $69,000,000 a year, but with tariff-free delivery and faster lead times. The government has warned the tariff could rise to 20% within 2 years. The board must decide whether to switch suppliers or stay with the Country F parts.

questions.question_text: Define 'multinational company (MNC)'.
questions.model_answer: A company that has operations or facilities in two or more countries [2].

knowledge_max_2: A company operating in more than one country
Has facilities/operations across national borders

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits for Kingsley Motor Group Plc of switching to union-based parts suppliers.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: No tariff on parts [k], avoiding the $7,200,000 a year the 12% tariff costs on $60,000,000 of imports [app]. Benefit 2: Faster, more reliable delivery [k], as union-based suppliers quoted tariff-free delivery with shorter lead times, reducing stock needs for the 24,000 vehicles built each year [app].

knowledge_max_2: Buying inside a customs union avoids the import tariff
Local/bloc sourcing shortens delivery times and improves reliability
application_max_2: 24,000 vehicles a year; union suppliers quote faster lead times

questions.question_text: Explain two problems for Kingsley Motor Group Plc of switching to union-based suppliers.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Higher parts prices [k], with union-based suppliers quoting about $69,000,000 a year, roughly $9,000,000 more than Country F imports [app], squeezing margins unless vehicle prices rise [an]. Problem 2: Limited supplier choice and quality risk [k], as the union has few qualified engine and gearbox makers [app], creating dependence on a small number of suppliers and possible delivery delays [an].

knowledge_max_2: Bloc-based inputs may cost more than non-bloc imports
Fewer qualified suppliers raises dependence and supply risk
application_max_2: Engines and gearboxes; few union-based manufacturers
analysis_max_2: Margins squeezed unless vehicle prices increase
Supply delays / over-reliance on a few suppliers hurt output

questions.question_text: Do you think Kingsley Motor Group Plc should switch parts sourcing to union-based suppliers inside the Valdonia Customs Union? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Switching removes the 12% tariff [k], saving $7,200,000 a year on parts worth $60,000,000 and shielding the plant if the tariff rises to 20% within 2 years, when the duty would cost $12,000,000 [app]; this would improve margins and protect the 1,800 jobs at the Country X plant [an]. However, staying with Country F keeps the lowest quoted price but relies on imports facing $7,200,000 to $12,000,000 of tariff costs [app], weakening competitiveness over time [an]. Free trade within a customs union lowers the cost of member-based sourcing [k]. Overall, Kingsley should switch to union-based suppliers because the saving beats the 15% price premium if the tariff rises to 20% [eval], although it should negotiate phased contracts to manage quality risk [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Sourcing inside a customs union avoids the common external tariff
Free trade agreements lower the cost of trade between members
application_max_2: $7,200,000 now rising to $12,000,000 if tariff hits 20%
Union quote $69,000,000 vs Country F $60,000,000; tariff-free delivery
analysis_max_2: Margins improve and 1,800 jobs are protected
Staying with Country F weakens competitiveness as tariffs rise
evaluation_max_2: Clear overall judgement with quantitative reasoning
Qualifies the switch with a risk-management condition

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Fernhollow Biscuit Co is a family-run biscuit manufacturer in Country X, a founding member of the Orin Trade Bloc. The firm has operated for 16 years, employs 52 staff and generates $2,750,000 in annual revenue. Around 80% of sales are in the home market, spread across 1,200 retail outlets nationwide.

A supermarket chain in Country B, a fellow Orin Trade Bloc member, has offered to list Fernhollow's shortbread in 300 of its stores, ordering 40,000 cases a year at $9.00 per case, worth $360,000 annually, shipped tariff-free. However, Country B already has three established biscuit makers and transport and insurance add $18,000 a year. Directors must decide between accepting the export contract or investing the same effort in expanding domestic distribution into 400 additional outlets.

questions.question_text: Define 'export'.
questions.model_answer: Selling goods or services to buyers in another country [2].

knowledge_max_2: Selling goods or services abroad
Buyers are in another/foreign country

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages for Fernhollow Biscuit Co of exporting shortbread to Country B.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: Tariff-free entry to Country B [k], because the Orin Trade Bloc removes duties between members, so Fernhollow's 40,000 cases a year at $9.00 per case arrive without added charges [app]. Advantage 2: New customer base [k], adding Country B's 300 stores to income alongside its $2,750,000 home-market sales [app].

knowledge_max_2: Exports to bloc members enter without tariffs
Exporting adds a new customer base / diversifies sales
application_max_2: 40,000 cases a year at $9.00; tariff-free within the Orin Trade Bloc
300 Country B stores to add to $2,750,000 home sales

questions.question_text: Explain two challenges for Fernhollow Biscuit Co of serving Country B.
questions.model_answer: Challenge 1: Strong local competition [k], as three established biscuit makers already supply Country B [app], forcing Fernhollow to spend heavily on promotion or undercut on price to win shelf space [an]. Challenge 2: Extra logistics costs [k], with transport and insurance adding $18,000 a year to the contract [app], cutting into the net gain from the $360,000 deal [an].

knowledge_max_2: Foreign markets have established local competitors
Exporting adds transport and insurance costs
application_max_2: Three established biscuit makers already supply Country B
$18,000 a year transport and insurance cost
analysis_max_2: Higher promotion spend or lower prices needed to win distribution

questions.question_text: Do you think Fernhollow Biscuit Co should accept the Country B export contract or expand domestic distribution into 400 more outlets? Justify your answer.

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Varrow Bay Fisheries Ltd is a fish processing business on the coast of Country X. The firm has operated for 12 years, employs 60 workers and generates $7,500,000 in annual revenue processing imported frozen cod into chilled fillets for supermarkets. It currently imports 5,500 tonnes of cod a year from Country D at $900 per tonne.

The Country X government has announced that the annual import quota for frozen cod will fall from 6,000 tonnes to 2,000 tonnes from January, to protect domestic fishing boats. Domestic cod costs $1,150 per tonne and only about 1,800 tonnes of spare catch is available. Shop cod prices are expected to rise from $4.00 to $5.00 per kilogram, around 25%. Directors must choose between signing contracts with domestic boats or investing $850,000 in Varrow Bay's own trawler.

Effect 2: Higher prices [k], as cod rises to $1,150 per tonne with only 1,800 tonnes of spare catch available [app], lifting revenue for domestic fishermen [an].

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Aldercombe Footwear Ltd is a private limited company that manufactures leather shoes in Country X. The factory has operated for 15 years, employs 75 workers and produces 85,000 pairs a year, generating $5,200,000 in annual revenue. Its best-selling shoe retails at $65, slightly above the $58 price of imported rivals from Country F.

The government has introduced a 22% tariff on imported footwear to protect domestic manufacturers. Imported rival shoes will now cost about $71 at the border, above Aldercombe's price. However, the tariff is temporary, with a review after 3 years, and some ministers warn protection breeds inefficiency. Directors are weighing whether to invest $1,100,000 in new lasting machines to cut production costs before the review, or to enjoy the shelter the tariff provides.

questions.question_text: Define 'trade barrier'.
questions.model_answer: Any government measure that restricts international trade, such as a tariff or quota [2].

knowledge_max_2: A government measure restricting international trade

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of the 22% tariff for Aldercombe Footwear Ltd.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Removes price undercutting [k], as imported rivals from Country F will now retail at about $71, above Aldercombe's $65 price [app]. Benefit 2: Higher sales volumes [k], as price-sensitive shoppers shift to the domestic 85,000 pairs Aldercombe can supply with 75 workers [app].

knowledge_max_2: Tariff raises import prices so domestic goods win on price
Domestic firms gain market share / higher sales volumes
application_max_2: Country F imports now about $71 vs Aldercombe's $65
Capacity of 85,000 pairs a year with 75 workers

questions.question_text: Explain two drawbacks of relying on the tariff for Aldercombe Footwear Ltd's success.
questions.model_answer: Drawback 1: Complacency risk [k], as shelter from competition may let inefficient working practices persist [app], weakening the firm before the government reviews the tariff after 3 years [an]. Drawback 2: Reduced consumer choice may shrink the market [k], as shoppers face higher prices and fewer imported styles [app], cutting total footwear demand in Country X and Aldercombe's own sales [an].

knowledge_max_2: Protection reduces the incentive to improve efficiency
Tariffs raise consumer prices and reduce choice
application_max_2: Tariff review after 3 years; inefficient practices may persist
Imported styles cost about $71, above Aldercombe's $65
analysis_max_2: Firm weakened / uncompetitive once the review happens
Total footwear demand falls / firm's own sales reduced

questions.question_text: Do you think the 22% import tariff is likely to benefit Aldercombe Footwear Ltd in the long run? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: The 22% tariff lifts Aldercombe Footwear Ltd above Country F imports, which now retail at about $71 against Aldercombe's $65 [app], lifting orders and protecting $5,200,000 revenue and 75 jobs in the short term [an]; tariffs are designed to protect domestic producers from cheaper foreign competition [k]. However, shelter can breed inefficiency, letting firms delay cutting costs [k]; the tariff is temporary, facing a review after 3 years [app], so Aldercombe could struggle if protection ends while its costs stay high [an]. Overall, the tariff will benefit Aldercombe in the long run only if it invests the $1,100,000 in new lasting machines during the 3-year protection [eval], because protection will expire and competition from Country F imports will return [eval].

Protection can breed inefficiency / delay cost-cutting

Tariff temporary with review after 3 years; $1,100,000 machine investment
analysis_max_2: Short-term protection of orders, revenue and employment
Competitiveness lost after the review if costs stay high
evaluation_max_2: Clear overall judgement on long-term benefit
Recognises conditions (investment) for tariff to bring lasting gains
